passages.happening:
“Next, have your brother Aaron brought to you from among the Israelites, along with his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, to serve Me as priests” (verse 1).

“Make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to give him glory and splendor” (verse 2). Skilled craftsmen, “whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom”, are to make them (verse 3).

“These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban, and a sash” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The plans turn from the building to the people who will serve in it. A holy God is coming to live in the middle of a people who sin. So who can come near? The answer here is a priesthood: men who stand between the people and God and represent each to the other. This chapter clothes them. The next chapter describes how they are set apart.

Notice the sharp turn in the larger story. While Moses is on the mountain receiving these plans for Aaron's clothing, Aaron himself is below making a golden calf (chapter 32).

The garments are for ‘glory and splendor’. They are costly: gold, fine linen, blue and purple dyed with the expensive dye of sea snails, scarlet, engraved gems. They mark a royal and holy service. The priest is not dressed to show off himself. He is dressed for the God he serves.

And the skill to make them is God's gift. The craftsmen are filled ‘with a spirit of wisdom’. Making beautiful things for God is treated as holy work.
passages.later:
Hebrews calls Jesus “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens” (Hebrews 4:14), one “who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

Peter extends the priesthood to all who belong to Christ: “you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood” (1 Peter 2:5).
passages.asks: God gave craftsmen a spirit of wisdom for making beautiful things. Ask whether you see your own skill, whatever it is, as a gift to be used for God. And ask what it would mean to do ordinary work for the glory of the God you serve.

passages.t: The ephod, and names on his shoulders
passages.happening:
“They are to make the ephod of finely spun linen embroidered with gold, and with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn” (verse 6), with two shoulder pieces and a woven waistband (verses 7-8).

“Take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel: six of their names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, in the order of their birth” (verses 9-10). They are set on the shoulder pieces “as memorial stones for the sons of Israel. Aaron is to bear their names on his two shoulders as a memorial before the LORD” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The ephod seems to have been a kind of apron or vest, held up by straps over the shoulders and a band at the waist. Elsewhere the word can mean a simple linen garment; the boy Samuel wore one.

On each shoulder was an onyx stone with six names of the tribes, engraved the way a seal was cut. A seal stood for its owner. So the people were carried by name, as if their own seals were on him.

When Aaron went into the holy place, he carried the whole people on his shoulders. No tribe was left outside.

‘A memorial before the LORD’ does not mean God would forget his people without it. It means the priest's work was to hold them before God.
passages.later:
Samuel served as a boy “wearing a linen ephod” (1 Samuel 2:18).

Isaiah hears God speak to his people in the same spirit: “Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands” (Isaiah 49:16).

Hebrews says of Christ: “He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
passages.asks: Aaron carried the names of all the tribes into God's presence. Ask whose names you carry to God in prayer, and whose you have stopped carrying. And ask what it means to you that Christ, in Hebrews' words, always lives to intercede for his people.

passages.happening:
“You are also to make a breastpiece of judgment with the same workmanship as the ephod” (verse 15). It is square, folded double, a span each way (verse 16). On it are four rows of three precious stones (verses 17-20). “The twelve stones are to correspond to the names of the sons of Israel, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes” (verse 21). It is fastened to the ephod with gold chains and blue cords (verses 22-28).

“Whenever Aaron enters the Holy Place, he shall bear the names of the sons of Israel over his heart on the breastpiece of judgment, as a continual reminder before the LORD” (verse 29). “And place the Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece of judgment, so that they will also be over Aaron’s heart whenever he comes before the LORD” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The breastpiece was a square pouch on the priest's chest, set with twelve gems, one for each tribe, each engraved with a tribe's name.

The names are on his shoulders and now over his heart as well.

What were the twelve stones? No one is sure. Ancient names for stones do not match modern names neatly, which is why Bibles translate them differently.

It is called the breastpiece of judgment, or of decision, because it held the Urim and Thummim. The text never describes them. Other passages show they were used to learn God's will in a matter, apparently giving yes or no, or choosing between answers. The words are often explained as meaning something like lights and perfections, though that too is debated. So the breastpiece joined two things: carrying the people before God, and seeking God's word for the people.
passages.later:
Later Joshua was to stand before Eleazar the priest, “who will seek counsel for him before the LORD by the judgment of the Urim” (Numbers 27:21). After the exile, the Urim and Thummim were no longer at hand: the governor ruled that some could not eat the holy food “until there was a priest to consult the Urim and Thummim” (Ezra 2:63).

The Song of Songs uses the picture of a seal over the heart for love: “Set me as a seal over your heart” (Song of Songs 8:6).

Revelation's new Jerusalem rests on foundations “adorned with every kind of precious stone” (Revelation 21:19).
passages.asks: The priest carried the people over his heart whenever he came before God. Ask whether you pray for others from duty, or from the heart. And ask how you seek God's guidance, and whether you are ready to hear an answer you did not want.

passages.t: The blue robe, and ‘HOLY TO THE LORD’
passages.happening:
“You are to make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue cloth” (verse 31), with a strong woven collar (verse 32). Around the hem go pomegranates of blue, purple and scarlet, “with gold bells between them” (verse 33).

“Aaron must wear the robe whenever he ministers, and its sound will be heard when he enters or exits the sanctuary before the LORD, so that he will not die” (verse 35).

“You are to make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it as on a seal: HOLY TO THE LORD” (verse 36). It is tied to the front of the turban with a blue cord (verse 37). “And it will be worn on Aaron’s forehead, so that he may bear the iniquity of the holy things that the sons of Israel consecrate with regard to all their holy gifts” (verse 38), “so that they may be acceptable before the LORD” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The robe was all blue, and its hem rang with bells as the priest moved.

Why the bells? The text says only that the sound was to be heard ‘so that he will not die’. Some think the bells let the people outside know the priest was still alive and serving. Others see them as announcing his coming into God's presence. The text leaves it there.

On his forehead was a gold plate engraved ‘HOLY TO THE LORD’. It did more than name him. It let him ‘bear the iniquity of the holy things’. Even the people's best gifts to God were not perfect. The priest carried their flaws so that the gifts could be accepted. The Hebrew verb for bearing guilt is the same verb that can mean to forgive. It comes back in God's great words about himself in 34:7.

Why so much detail, and why the warnings of death? Because the tabernacle and its priests answer the central problem of Exodus: how a holy God can live among a sinful people without destroying them. Holiness is real. It is dangerous to the unholy. The story shows this when two of Aaron's sons die for offering fire God had not commanded.
passages.later:
Leviticus tells it: “So fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed them” (Leviticus 10:2).

Zechariah looks to a day when holiness reaches ordinary things: “On that day, HOLY TO THE LORD will be inscribed on the bells of the horses” (Zechariah 14:20).

Hebrews says of Christ: “Unlike the other high priests, He does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people; He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself” (Hebrews 7:27).
passages.asks: The gold plate carried the flaws in the people's best gifts. Ask whether you believe God can accept what you offer him, flawed as it is. And ask what it would mean for ‘holy to the LORD’ to be written on the ordinary things of your life.

passages.happening:
“You are to weave the tunic with fine linen, make the turban of fine linen, and fashion an embroidered sash” (verse 39). “Make tunics, sashes, and headbands for Aaron’s sons, to give them glory and splendor” (verse 40).

“After you put these garments on your brother Aaron and his sons, anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them so that they may serve Me as priests” (verse 41).

“Make linen undergarments to cover their bare flesh, extending from waist to thigh” (verse 42). They must wear them whenever they serve, “so that they will not incur guilt and die” (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
Aaron's sons wear simpler garments, but they too are for ‘glory and splendor’.

Verse 41 uses three words for setting them apart: anoint, ordain, consecrate. ‘Ordain’ is, word for word, to fill the hand, the Hebrew way of putting someone into office. In chapter 29 Moses will fill the priests' hands with portions of the offerings.

The linen undergarments protected modesty at the altar, as the ban on steps had done (20:26). They may also have set Israel's worship apart from rites of other peoples in which nakedness had a religious role.

These garments shaped the high priest's dress for centuries. The Jewish historian Josephus, in the first century, describes the high priest of his own day in the ephod, the breastpiece, the blue robe with bells and the gold plate. After the temple fell in AD 70 that service ended, and Jewish life carried the law forward through study and interpretation.
passages.later:
Peter speaks of the whole church as priests: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Revelation shows the risen Christ “dressed in a long robe, with a golden sash around His chest” (Revelation 1:13).

The New Testament reads the priesthood as a pattern pointing to Christ, not as a hidden prediction, and Hebrews never treats Aaron's service as false. A shadow, as the site's notes on Hebrews 8 say, is real.
passages.asks: Every priest, high or ordinary, was dressed by God for service. Ask what God has given you to wear, in character and calling, for the service he has given you. And ask how you treat holy things, and whether you come to God with care.
